opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the short version is that the metrics that seem to produce emergence tend to be nonlinear or discontinuous in how they score a model's outputs. The classic example is exact match. If you're asking a model to do, say, multi-digit arithmetic, exact match gives you full credit only if every single token is correct and zero otherwise. There's no partial credit.

What we found is that if you look underneath at something like the per-token probability of the correct answer, or the per-token error rate, that quantity tends to improve quite smoothly and predictably as you scale the model. But when you push that smooth improvement through a harsh metric, where you need, say, ten tokens all correct, you're effectively raising the per-token accuracy to the power of the sequence length. That compounding turns a gradual curve into something that looks flat for a long time and then shoots up sharply. And that sharp rise is what people were calling emergence.

So the distinguishing feature is really that the metric scales the underlying performance in a nonlinear or discontinuous way. Multiple-choice grade is another example: you get credit only if the correct option has the highest probability, which is a thresholding operation. When we swapped those for continuous or linear metrics, like token edit distance or Brier score, on the same model outputs, the abrupt jumps largely went away and you saw smooth, predictable improvement.

There's a second piece that matters too, which is resolution. A lot of these evaluations had relatively small test sets, so you couldn't measure very small but nonzero accuracies for the smaller models. They just read as zero. When we increased the amount of test data so we could actually resolve those small values, the smaller models were above chance, and again the curve looked much more continuous.

So I'd frame it this way. Emergence, at least in many of the cases people pointed to, is partly a property of the researcher's choice of measurement rather than some fundamental change in the model's behavior at a particular scale. That doesn't mean nothing interesting is happening, or that sharp transitions can never be real. But it does mean we should be careful, because the metric choice can manufacture the appearance of a sudden, unpredictable capability when the underlying progress is actually fairly predictable.

r001.rationale: The response identifies all-or-nothing scoring as a distinguishing feature, explaining that exact match gives full credit only when every token is correct and zero otherwise, with no partial credit.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that jumped out at us pretty quickly when we started digging into this is that the metrics people use when they claim emergence tend to share one property: they're nonlinear or discontinuous in the thing the model is actually getting better at. And what I mean by that is, think about something like exact match accuracy on a multi-step arithmetic problem, or a multiple-choice task where you only get credit if the full answer is correct. The model might be improving its per-token error rate smoothly and gradually as you scale it up, but the metric only registers that improvement once every single token in the sequence is right. So if you've got, say, a five-digit addition problem, and the model goes from being right on each digit 80 percent of the time to 90 percent to 99 percent, the per-token story is very smooth. But the all-or-nothing metric looks flat, flat, flat, and then suddenly jumps, because the probability of getting all the digits right is the product, and that product stays near zero until the per-token accuracy gets quite high.

So the distinguishing feature, in short, is that the metric is throwing away partial credit. It's a step function, or close to one, over what's really a continuous underlying capability. And the flip side is also true: when you swap in a metric that is linear or continuous in the underlying quantity, something like token edit distance, or Brier score instead of accuracy for multiple choice, those same tasks, on those same models, with the same outputs, stop looking emergent. The curves become smooth and predictable, and you can often extrapolate them from the smaller models. So that was kind of the crux of the argument for us. It's not that the models aren't getting better, they clearly are, it's that the sharpness and the unpredictability that people were attributing to the model were, in a lot of these cases, really properties of the researcher's choice of measurement.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that it interacts with how many test examples you have. If your metric is discontinuous and your test set is small, you get very high variance at the low-performance end, so small models look like they're at zero, and that makes the jump look even more dramatic than it is. Once you increase the resolution, either with more examples or with a finer-grained metric, a lot of that goes away.

r001.rationale: The response identifies all-or-nothing metrics that throw away partial credit as the distinguishing feature, and explains that this can make smooth improvement appear as emergence.

astra-6.text:
The distinguishing feature is often that the metric is discontinuous. Think about exact-match accuracy: the model gets no credit until it produces the entire answer correctly. It could be improving steadily—getting more pieces of the answer right—but the metric hides that progress until it crosses a threshold. Then you see what looks like a sudden jump in capability.

If you instead measure something more continuous, like the probability the model assigns to the correct answer, you may see a much smoother improvement. So the question is, how much of the emergence is a property of the model, and how much is a property of how we measure it? That doesn’t mean the capability isn’t useful or the jump isn’t meaningful. It means we need to be careful about inferring a sudden underlying change from that curve alone.

r001.rationale: The response identifies discontinuous, all-or-nothing scoring: exact-match gives no credit until the full answer is correct, hiding partial progress.

sol-6.1.text:
One distinguishing feature is that they tend to be discontinuous or nonlinear. Think about exact-match accuracy: the model gets credit only if the entire answer is correct. It can be improving steadily in the probabilities it assigns to the right tokens, but that improvement doesn’t show up in the metric until it crosses that threshold. Then you see what looks like a sudden jump.

So we have to distinguish a discontinuity in the model’s capabilities from a discontinuity introduced by how we measure them. If you look at a more continuous measure, like the probability assigned to the correct answer, you may see a much smoother progression. That doesn’t mean every claim of emergence goes away, but it does mean the choice of metric is central to interpreting it.

r001.rationale: It identifies exact-match scoring as all-or-nothing: credit comes only when the entire answer is correct, so partial improvement earns no metric credit.
